Two quick things from your list you could try right now:

Okay — here are simple, guided steps for box breathing. Read or follow each line slowly and repeat the cycle 4–6 times.

1) Sit comfortably with your back supported and feet on the floor (or lie down).  
2) Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of 4 — fill your belly, then your chest.  
3) Hold that breath for a count of 4.  
4) Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of 4, emptying your lungs.  
5) Hold the empty breath for a count of 4.  
6) Repeat steps 2–5 for about 1–3 minutes (4–6 cycles). Stop when you feel calmer.

Want me to time a single 1-minute or 2-minute round for you, or do you prefer to do it on your own? Also — would you like to check in the current situation into the circumstances log?

Good — thanks. A couple of options from your list that fit this situation:

- Block out a whole day for gentle self-care (plan_wellness_day). Fits because you said you’re exhausted and flat — a dedicated low-pressure day can give space to recover.  
- Work in small chunks and stop when you notice you are tired (activity_pacing). Fits because you’re tired now and pacing prevents pushing into deeper exhaustion.

If you want to plan recovery now, walk-through you can follow (quick, pick what feels doable):

1. Pick a target day and time window (today evening or one day this week). Keep it realistic — a half-day is fine.  
2. Decide three “must-have” low-effort items (examples: good meal, 30–45 minute walk, 1 hour of restful activity like reading or a warm bath). Limit to three so it doesn’t feel like a to-do list.  
3. Set boundaries: announce to anyone who needs to know (or block calendar/turn off notifications) and mark it as “no work.”  
4. Plan simple logistics now (what to eat, what to wear, any bookings). Remove tiny friction so you’ll follow through.  
5. Build in rest pockets: alternate short activity with 20–30 minute rest or quiet time so you don’t rebound into wired exhaustion.  
6. End with an easy wind-down (dim lights, gentle music) and one small check-in with yourself: what felt better, what you might change next time.

messages.content:
Got it — you’re exhausted, slept badly, and had calls all day. Here are two short things from your list to calm down right now:

- Box breathing: breathe in for 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4 for a minute.  
- Progressive muscle relaxation: tense major muscle groups for a few seconds, then release, working through the body for about 5 minutes.

Want to try one now, or would you prefer a different option?
yeah fine do the box breathing one. just tell me the steps.

Okay — box breathing. Do this slowly and gently:

1. Sit comfortably with feet on the floor and hands relaxed.  
2. Breathe in through your nose for a slow count of 4.  
3. Hold that breath for a count of 4.  
4. Breathe out through your mouth for a count of 4.  
5. Hold the empty breath for a count of 4.  
6. Repeat the cycle for about 1–3 minutes (or until you feel calmer).

Would you like to check in the current situation into the circumstances log?
no its already on my list. my eyes hurt from screens, what fixes that?

Two quick, simple things that can help screen-hurting eyes right now:

- Try the 20-20-20 rule — every 20 minutes look at something about 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds to relax focusing muscles and encourage blinking. Source: American Optometric Association. https://www.aoa.org/healthy-eyes/eye-and-vision-conditions/computer-vision-syndrome. ([aoa.org](https://www.aoa.org/healthy-eyes/eye-and-vision-conditions/computer-vision-syndrome?utm_source=openai))

- Use a warm compress + gentle eyelid massage for 5–10 minutes to loosen oils and relieve dry, gritty eyes (do the massage toward the lash line after the compress). Source: NHS / Frimley Health dry eye advice. https://www.fhft.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-library/dry-eye. ([fhft.nhs.uk](https://www.fhft.nhs.uk/patients-and-visitors/patient-information-library/dry-eye?utm_source=openai))

Both fit your situation: the first is a quick in-place habit to reduce strain during calls, the second targets the sore/dry feeling from long screen use. Want me to add one of these to your measures list?

messages.content:
Good idea — I can help add that. A quick note about the idea itself: one real strength is that a checklist makes evenings predictable and removes decision fatigue; one limit is it can feel like another item on your to-do list if it’s too long or rigid.

I checked your existing measures — nothing called “wind-down checklist” yet, though you do have an “energy_audit_redistribute_tasks” (more about moving tasks) and a “post_event_triage_checklist” (short recovery steps after an event).

I suggest a short measure sentence like: "Wind-down checklist for tonight: dim lights, put screens away 30 minutes before bed, pick one relaxing activity, and prep tomorrow’s must-dos." Want me to add that wording to your list? (Yes to add, or say edit if you want to change it.)
sure walk me through it

Great — let’s do a simple, low-effort wind-down you can actually follow tonight. I’ll keep it short so it doesn’t feel like extra work.

Tonight’s quick plan (pick or skip items as you like)
- 60–30 minutes before bed: dim the lights and lower the noise level.  
- 30 minutes before bed: put screens away or switch them to night mode; set a physical timer or an alarm labeled “wind-down.”  
- 20–10 minutes before bed: do one relaxing activity you enjoy (read a few pages, gentle stretching, warm drink, 10-minute walk).  
- 5 minutes before bed: jot down 1–3 must-dos for tomorrow so your mind can let go.  
- Bed time: use a short routine cue (brush teeth, wash face, deep breath) to signal sleep time.

Small ways to make it easier
- Keep the checklist visible (phone lock screen, sticky note, or a short text file).  
- Make the “one relaxing activity” something you actually want, not what you think you should do.  
- If you’re too tired to follow everything, just pick the 30-minute screen break and the 1–3 things note — that alone helps.

Quick test suggestion: try this tonight and notice how you feel in the morning. If it’s helpful, we can add a single-line measure to your list so you can reuse it.

Do you want me to add the short measure I suggested earlier to your list as written? (Yes to add, edit to change wording, or no to skip.)
yes please

Here are two quick things that fit “winding down”:

Great — box breathing. Steps:

1. Sit comfortably with feet on the floor and hands relaxed. If you’re lying down that’s fine too.  
2. Close your eyes (if comfortable) and breathe normally for a few seconds.  
3. Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of 4.  
4. Hold that breath for a count of 4.  
5. Exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of 4.  
6. Hold the empty breath for a count of 4.  
7. Repeat the cycle for about 1 minute to start (4–6 cycles). If that feels helpful, keep going up to 5 minutes.

messages.content:
Thanks — I hear you. Two ideas from your list that fit this well:

- Progressive muscle relaxation — a ~5-minute sequence of tensing and releasing major muscle groups to drop physical tension and help you feel ready for sleep.  
- Digital reset — unplug from screens for a few minutes before bed to reduce stimulation and make it easier to switch off.

Want me to walk you through the 5-minute progressive muscle relaxation now, or would you prefer the quick screen-free routine?
